proposals.quote_modern: mixed them a mess with cheese
proposals.replacement: mixed them a brew with cheese
proposals.butler: mixed them a mess with cheese, honey, meal, and Pramnian wine
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier ¶16 'mixed them a mess with cheese, honey, meal, and Pramnian wine' (word, pause, medium): read as 'made them a mixed dish or drink', with the note "'mess' = a dish of food and 'meal' = ground grain; both have misleading modern meanings". Book-level note 2 puts "'mess' (a dish)" first among the older meanings that mislead a modern reader.
proposals.reason: False friend (named in the brief's sweep list). Butler's 'mess' is a prepared portion of food or drink, a sense that survives only in 'mess hall' and 'a mess of pottage'. Today's reader hears disorder or dirt, so the hospitable drink Circe mixes becomes 'a mess', a comic and faintly disgusting picture Butler does not paint, and the reader had to guess between dish and drink. The thing is Homer's kykeon (named at 10.290 and 10.316): wine stirred with cheese, barley meal and honey, which 'they had drunk' in the next sentence. 'brew' is the plain current word for a drink mixed from several ingredients. It keeps Butler's verb 'mixed', his 'with' and his list. It is also neutral about the drugging, which Butler adds separately ('but she drugged it'), so his 'but' keeps its force; 'potion' would announce the drug before Butler does. The package already replaces false friends of this kind (Book 4: 'shambles' → 'slaughterhouse', 'toils' → 'net'). Apply together with B10-02 and B10-03, so that Butler's one word has one rendering in the Book.
proposals.collision_check: Butler's ¶16 has no 'brew', and 'brew' appears nowhere in his Book X; his only 'brewing' is the figurative 'mischief brewing' in Books II and III. 'drink' was rejected because Butler's 'when they had drunk' ends the same Butler sentence, which would put two of his words on one modern word. 'mixture' would echo his own 'mixed'. 'meal' (the ingredient) is untouched.

proposals.quote_modern: She will mix a mess for you to drink
proposals.replacement: She will mix a brew for you to drink
proposals.butler: She will mix a mess for you to drink
proposals.reader_evidence: Not flagged at ¶22. The paraphrase ('she will give Odysseus a drugged drink') shows 'for you to drink' carried the sense. The word was flagged at ¶16, and book-level note 2 flags it for the whole Book.
proposals.reason: The same Butler word for the same thing: Hermes forecasts the drink of ¶16. Once ¶16 is repaired, leaving 'mess' here would give one Butler word two renderings in one Book, the defect the package's steady-word rows exist to prevent. 'mix a mess' also reads today as 'make a mess'. The rest of the sentence, including Butler's 'meal' and 'for you to drink', is untouched.
proposals.collision_check: Butler's ¶22 has 'drink' as a verb in this very clause ('for you to drink'), which is why the noun cannot be 'drink'. There is no 'brew' in his ¶22. His 'meal', 'drug', 'charm' and 'virtue' in the paragraph are unaffected.

proposals.quote_modern: she mixed a mess in a golden goblet
proposals.replacement: she mixed a brew in a golden goblet
proposals.butler: she mixed a mess in a golden goblet for me to drink
proposals.reader_evidence: Not flagged at ¶24. The paraphrase ('gave him a drugged drink in a golden cup') shows 'goblet ... for me to drink' carried the sense. This is the brief's own known example (10.24).
proposals.reason: Of the three, 'a mess in a golden goblet' is the sharpest clash: the modern sense turns the goddess's drink into slops just as the paragraph stresses its luxury (a silver-inlaid seat, a footstool, a golden goblet). The rendering is the same as B10-01 and B10-02. 'fared onward' in the same paragraph is ruled on separately and kept (see rejected_barriers).
proposals.collision_check: Butler's ¶24 has 'drink' ('for me to drink') and 'drunk' ('I had drunk it'), so again not 'drink'. There is no 'brew'. 'fared onward' and Butler's 'walked' in the same paragraph are untouched.

rejected_barriers.quote: mend me this mischief

rejected_barriers.quote: I will help no man whom heaven hates

rejected_barriers.quote: a man who could do without sleep might earn double wages
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly. 'one wage ... and another' was already clarified at the 2026-09-23 round.

rejected_barriers.quote: As for the others, there was not one of them left

rejected_barriers.reason: Names (context note). The reader parsed 'by Perse' correctly.

rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's rendering of Homer's 'in silence', and the reader read 'in silence'. Homer and Butler leave the reason for the silence unstated.

rejected_barriers.quote: we are not going to die so much before our time after all

rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's content.

rejected_barriers.quote: I went as high as I could this morning
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's own inconsistency, printed exactly as he has it ('I went as high as I could this morning'); the pilot review (review-2026-09-23/pilot-book10-findings.md) praised keeping it. Per the task, it is not changed, because the modern wording does not depart from Butler.

rejected_barriers.quote: Their hearts sank as they heard me
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's implication. The reader made the connection.

rejected_barriers.quote: Then we cast lots in a helmet, and the lot fell on Eurylochus
rejected_barriers.reason: The next sentence ('So he set out with his twenty-two men') shows what the lot decided, as in Butler, and the reader read it correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: on a site that could be seen from far off, in the middle of the forest
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's own description (a place visible all round), read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: poor bewitched creatures whom she had tamed by her enchantments and drugged into submission
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer leaves this open, and ¶34 hints at it. Resolving it would add interpretation.

rejected_barriers.quote: making a web so fine
rejected_barriers.reason: 'web' meaning woven cloth is current in the textile sense, and the same sentence says 'loom' and 'weave'. Read correctly with high confidence. D29: Butler's word.

rejected_barriers.quote: beech mast
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's 'beech masts', set as the standard mass noun. 'acorns' and 'such as pigs eat' fix the sense, and the reader's reading, nuts fallen from beech trees, is right.

rejected_barriers.quote: I am most urgently bound to do so
rejected_barriers.reason: 'bound' meaning obliged is current ('duty-bound'), and 'most urgently' rules out 'certain to'. Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: I met Hermes with his golden wand, disguised as a young man
rejected_barriers.reason: Homer's narrator speaks with hindsight. Not a text defect.

rejected_barriers.quote: Take this herb, which is one of great virtue
rejected_barriers.reason: 'virtue' meaning the power of a thing is current if formal ('by virtue of'). The next sentence says what the herb does, and the reader read it correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: she will drug the meal she makes it with
rejected_barriers.reason: Kept (D29), and kept as one rendering for Butler's one word in this Book. 'meal' meaning ground grain is current ('oatmeal', 'cornmeal'). ¶16's ingredient list (cheese, honey, meal, wine) sets the sense, and ¶43's 'white barley meal' confirms it. The reader resolved it by recalling ¶16. Changing it here alone would give Butler's 'meal' two renderings in the Book, and 'barley' is not Butler's word here (the pilot review rejected 'barley meal' at ¶16). Which ingredient carries the drug is a detail; the story needs only that the drink is drugged, and the sentence says so.

rejected_barriers.quote: she will strip you of your manhood and leave you helpless
rejected_barriers.reason: Whether the threat is literal or figurative is Homer's own ambiguity (10.301, anenora, 'unmanned'). The reader got the sense, loss of manhood or strength. The wording was set by the 2026-09-23 accessibility edit. See recurring for the broken echo with ¶26.

rejected_barriers.quote: while I fared onward to the house of Circe
rejected_barriers.reason: Not flagged; a known example from the brief (10.24), kept. 'fare' as a verb of motion is literary but still in current dictionaries ('fare forth', 'wayfarer'), and 'onward to the house of Circe' supplies the direction, so the sense 'went on' cannot be missed. The reader paraphrased it 'went on to Circe's house'. It is Butler's own word, restored at the Book 10 collision check (book10/continuity.md §7, P025 = ¶24) because 'went on' collided with Butler's 'went back' in the same sentence, which is D29's preferred kind of repair. The Book's other two forms of 'fare' (¶10 'fare like the rest', ¶37 'how badly you have fared') are Butler's own, in the current sense, and are unaffected. If the lead still wants a plainer verb, 'pressed on' collides with nothing in Butler's ¶24, but it adds a note of effort that Butler's neutral 'fared' lacks, so it is not recommended; 'walked on' would merge Butler's 'fared' with his 'walked along' in the same sentence.

rejected_barriers.quote: clasped my knees
rejected_barriers.reason: A gesture of supplication, Homer's. Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: a taste of the herb I gave you
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's 'herb' for Circe's drug; Homer uses one word for both the drug and Hermes's herb. 'I gave you' marks it as hers, and the reader read it correctly. 'drug' here would merge Butler's 'drugs' and 'herb' in this paragraph (collision rule, second clause).

rejected_barriers.quote: will unman me and make me fit for nothing
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words ('unman me and make me fit for nothing'), read in the right sense. Whether the threat is literal or figurative is Homer's own ambiguity. See recurring for the ¶22/¶26 echo.

recurring.item: unman ... fit for nothing (Hermes's warning, which Odysseus repeats to Circe)
recurring.rendering: no comprehension repair. Note for the lead: the 2026-09-23 accessibility edit changed ¶22 to 'strip you of your manhood and leave you helpless', while ¶26 keeps Butler's 'unman me and make me fit for nothing', so Butler's verbatim echo is now two renderings. The reader was equally unsure at both, because the literal-or-figurative doubt is Homer's own, so the edit did not make the threat clearer. If the lead wants the echo back, the option that collides with nothing is ¶26 'will strip me of my manhood and leave me helpless'.

summary: Book 10 is already highly comprehensible. In all 49 paragraphs the blind reader's paraphrase matches Butler, and none of the 69 barriers is a misreading. The 18 barriers marked unsure are Homer's content (the floating island, the Laestrygonians' short nights, whether Circe's beasts were once men, the literal or figurative threat to Odysseus's manhood, the underworld names and rites), customs and gestures, and names from other Books. The 'continuity gaps' the reader noticed ('this morning' ¶13, 'the men who had been left behind' ¶37, the reprimand, the promise) are Butler's own words printed unchanged, so they stay. The one real problem is the false friend 'mess' for Circe's mixed drink (¶16, ¶22, ¶24). The word now means disorder or dirt, the reader had to guess between dish and drink, and 'a mess in a golden goblet' reads as comic, so it is repaired as a set with 'brew' (recommended). 'fared onward' (¶24) was read correctly and is Butler's own word, restored to avoid a collision, so it is kept. 'meal', 'virtue', 'bound', 'web', 'fountain' and 'mischief' are old senses that their own sentences carry, and the reader read each correctly. There are two notes for the lead, neither a comprehension repair. Book 9 keeps 'livelong day' where this Book prints 'whole long day'. The 2026-09-23 edit at ¶22 split Butler's verbatim echo of the 'unman ... fit for nothing' warning, which ¶26 still prints, without making the threat any clearer.
